question: How does TCP connection termination work, and why does it use four steps instead of three?

key_points: FIN from initiator
ACK from receiver
FIN from receiver when it's also done
final ACK from initiator

reference_solution.sample_answer: Either side can initiate termination by sending a FIN. The other side ACKs it, but may still have data to send, so it sends its own FIN later, which gets ACKed by the original side. It's 4 steps because each direction of the full-duplex connection needs to be closed independently, unlike setup where both directions can be confirmed together. The closing side enters TIME_WAIT to handle any lingering packets.

question: Explain TCP congestion control, including slow start and congestion avoidance.

key_points: congestion window grows exponentially in slow start
switches to linear growth after threshold (congestion avoidance)
packet loss signals congestion, window shrinks
protects the network, not just the receiver
reference_solution.sample_answer: TCP starts conservatively with a small congestion window and doubles it each round trip during slow start, probing available bandwidth quickly. Once it hits a threshold (or detects loss), it switches to congestion avoidance, growing the window linearly instead. On packet loss, TCP assumes congestion and cuts the window sharply, then ramps back up. This whole mechanism protects the shared network from being overwhelmed, unlike flow control which protects the receiver.

question: What problem does the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) solve in a switched Ethernet network?

This gives you physical redundancy for failover without ever having an actual active loop in the network at the same time.

question: Beyond just running over UDP, what specific improvements does QUIC (the transport underlying HTTP/3) make over traditional TCP?

reference_solution.sample_answer: QUIC combines what used to be separate TCP and TLS handshakes into a single, faster handshake, and supports 0-RTT connection resumption for a client reconnecting to a server it's talked to recently. QUIC also identifies connections by a connection ID instead of the traditional IP-and-port tuple, so a connection can survive a client switching networks, like moving from Wi-Fi to cellular, without needing to reconnect. question: HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests over a single TCP connection to fix HTTP/1.1's head-of-line blocking. Why can head-of-line blocking still occur at the TCP level even with HTTP/2?

reference_solution.sample_answer: HTTP/2 solves head-of-line blocking at the application layer by multiplexing independent request/response streams over a single TCP connection instead of needing one connection per request. The catch is that TCP itself guarantees strictly in-order byte delivery to the application, so if a single packet is lost, TCP withholds every packet that arrived after it — even ones belonging to a completely unrelated HTTP/2 stream — until the lost packet is retransmitted and the order is restored. That reintroduces head-of-line blocking, just one layer down, at the TCP level instead of the HTTP level, and it's exactly the problem QUIC was built to fix, since QUIC tracks loss and reordering per-stream instead of for the whole connection.

reference_solution.sample_answer: Quality of Service lets network equipment treat certain traffic with priority over other traffic specifically when a link doesn't have enough capacity for everything trying to use it at once. This is commonly used to protect latency-sensitive traffic, like voice or video calls, from being delayed behind large, latency-tolerant bulk transfers competing for the same link. It's worth noting that QoS only actually changes behavior when there's real contention for bandwidth — on a link with plenty of spare capacity, prioritization markings don't visibly change anything.

question: What is the difference between port forwarding and NAT itself?

by default, NAT has no rule for routing unsolicited inbound connections to any specific internal device

reference_solution.sample_answer: NAT, by default, only really handles outbound connections cleanly: it translates many internal private IP addresses to one shared public IP so internal devices can reach the internet, and it tracks those outbound connections to correctly route their replies back inside. Port forwarding is a manually configured rule layered on top of that, telling the router 'traffic arriving on external port X should always be routed to this specific internal device and port', which is what lets you host something like a home game server or a personal web server that's reachable from outside your own network.

question: What's the difference between a volumetric (network-layer) DDoS attack and an application-layer DDoS attack, and how do basic mitigations differ?

question: What are SYN cookies, and how do they let a server defend against a SYN flood attack without keeping per-connection state?

no per-connection memory is reserved until the final ACK arrives with a sequence number that validates back to a legitimate cookie
this means a flood of fake SYNs that never complete the handshake costs the server almost no memory, since nothing was ever allocated for them

SYN cookies sidestep this by not allocating any state at all when the SYN arrives: instead, the server cryptographically encodes the connection information directly into the sequence number it sends back in the SYN-ACK. If a legitimate final ACK arrives, its acknowledgment number lets the server reconstruct and validate the original connection details from just that packet, so no memory ever needed to be reserved for the many fake, never-completed connections a flood generates. The trade-off is that some TCP options normally remembered from the original SYN can't survive being encoded into a cookie, which is one reason servers often only switch to SYN cookies once their normal connection backlog queue is already under real pressure.

question: What is certificate pinning, and what are its trade-offs for a mobile app that talks to a backend API?

key_points: normally a client trusts any certificate signed by a certificate authority in its trust store
certificate pinning hardcodes the expected certificate (or its public key) for a specific server, rejecting connections even if a technically valid but unexpected certificate is presented

reference_solution.sample_answer: Normally, a client trusts any server certificate as long as it's validly signed by a certificate authority already in its trust store — certificate pinning tightens that by hardcoding the specific certificate, or its public key, that the app expects from a given server, and rejecting the connection if anything else is presented, even a technically valid certificate from a legitimate CA. This protects against the scenario of a compromised or coerced certificate authority issuing a fraudulent but technically valid certificate for your domain, which pinning would simply reject. The serious downside is certificate rotation: if you ever need to change the pinned certificate, for expiry or after a compromise, any already-installed app version that still has the old pin hardcoded will completely fail to connect, potentially bricking connectivity for users who haven't updated. In practice, this means pinning needs careful planning, like pinning to a more stable intermediate CA or supporting multiple valid pins simultaneously during a rotation window.

question: Explain the TLS certificate chain of trust: root CA, intermediate CA, and leaf certificate. Why do we need intermediates at all instead of the root signing every website's certificate directly?

the root's private key signs intermediate CA certificates, and intermediates sign the actual leaf (server) certificates websites use

using intermediates lets the root CA's extremely sensitive private key stay offline and rarely used, since it only ever signs a small number of intermediates
if an intermediate is ever compromised, it can be revoked without needing to revoke and redistribute trust in the root itself, which would be far more disruptive
reference_solution.sample_answer: The root CA's certificate is the ultimate trust anchor, pre-installed in every operating system and browser's trust store, and its private key is used to sign intermediate CA certificates rather than website certificates directly. Those intermediates then sign the actual leaf certificates that individual websites present, and a client validates trust by walking the chain from the website's leaf certificate up through however many intermediates to a root it already trusts. The reason for this layering is operational security: the root's private key is so sensitive that it's kept offline and used as rarely as possible, only to sign a handful of intermediates, rather than being exposed to sign every website's certificate directly. It also means that if an intermediate CA is ever compromised, it can be revoked on its own without needing to revoke and redistribute trust in the root itself, which would be a far more disruptive event affecting every certificate the root has ever signed.

question: How does HTTP/2 multiplexing specifically solve the head-of-line blocking problem that existed at the application layer in HTTP/1.1?

question: In a service mesh, every service-to-service call is routed through a sidecar proxy. What are the network-level latency implications of this design?

reference_solution.sample_answer: In a service mesh, a call from service A to service B doesn't go directly — it hops from A's application to A's local sidecar proxy, across the network to B's local sidecar proxy, and finally to B's application code, adding two extra hops compared to a direct call. That latency cost buys uniform mTLS, retries, and observability without touching each service's own code, which is usually worth it, but for especially latency-sensitive call paths with many hops, the cumulative sidecar overhead is real and worth actually benchmarking rather than assuming it's negligible.

question: What is bufferbloat, and why can it cause noticeable latency spikes even on a connection with plenty of available bandwidth?

key_points: network equipment (routers, modems) often has oversized buffers meant to avoid dropping packets during brief bursts
when a link is saturated, those large buffers fill up and queue packets rather than dropping them, adding significant queuing delay before packets are even sent
TCP relies on packet loss as a congestion signal; oversized buffers delay that loss signal, so senders keep sending well past the point they should have slowed down
the result is high latency (bufferbloat) on an otherwise high-bandwidth connection, since packets are stuck waiting in a deep queue rather than being dropped early to trigger a congestion response
mitigations include smart queue management algorithms (e.g. CoDel) that intentionally drop or signal congestion earlier, before queues grow deep enough to cause this delay
reference_solution.sample_answer: Bufferbloat happens because network equipment, like home routers or ISP modems, often has larger packet buffers than is actually good for latency, under the reasonable-sounding assumption that bigger buffers avoid dropping packets during brief traffic bursts. The problem is that when the link is genuinely saturated, those oversized buffers just fill up and queue packets for a long time before sending them, rather than dropping any — and since TCP relies on packet loss as its main signal that it's sending too fast, that delayed loss signal means senders keep sending well past the point where they should have already slowed down, all while packets pile up in the queue. The end result is a connection with plenty of raw bandwidth but terrible latency, because every packet is stuck waiting behind a long queue rather than actually being congested in the traditional loss-based sense — modern mitigations like the CoDel queue management algorithm address this by deliberately signaling congestion earlier, before the queue gets deep enough to cause this delay.

question: What's the difference between a broadcast domain and a collision domain, and how do switches and routers each affect them?

key_points: a collision domain is the set of devices whose transmissions could collide with each other on a shared medium
a broadcast domain is the set of devices that receive a broadcast frame sent by any one of them
a switch creates a separate collision domain per port, but by default all switch ports remain in the same broadcast domain
a router (or VLAN boundary) is what actually separates broadcast domains, since routers don't forward broadcast frames between networks
understanding this distinction matters for diagnosing both performance issues (collisions) and broadcast storm/scalability issues (broadcast domain size)
reference_solution.sample_answer: A collision domain is the set of devices where two transmissions happening at the same time could collide with each other, which mattered a lot on old shared-medium Ethernet and hubs, but a modern switch gives each individual port its own separate collision domain, effectively eliminating collisions in practice. A broadcast domain is a different, larger concept: it's the set of devices that will all receive a broadcast frame sent by any single device in that domain, and a switch, by default, keeps every one of its ports in the same broadcast domain even though it's already split them into separate collision domains. What actually separates broadcast domains is a router, or equivalently a VLAN boundary enforced by a layer-3 device, since routers simply don't forward broadcast frames from one network into another — this distinction matters because a very large broadcast domain, even with zero collisions, can still suffer from broadcast traffic overhead at scale.

reference_solution.sample_answer: IP masquerading is a specific flavor of source NAT designed for outbound-only connectivity from a private network to the internet, where many internal private IP addresses all get translated to appear as if they're coming from the router's own single public IP address. question: What is MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching), and why do ISPs and large enterprise networks still use it?

key_points: MPLS forwards packets based on a short, fixed-length label rather than doing a full IP routing table lookup at every hop
labels are attached at the network's edge and swapped (not re-looked-up from scratch) at each intermediate router along a pre-determined path

reference_solution.sample_answer: MPLS forwards packets based on a short, fixed-length label attached to each packet, rather than doing a full routing table lookup by IP address at every single hop — labels are attached once at the network's edge and simply swapped, not recomputed, at each router along a path that was already determined ahead of time. This label-swapping approach is faster and more predictable than full IP lookups everywhere, and importantly lets network operators engineer exactly which physical path certain traffic takes, rather than just trusting standard IP routing to pick a path on its own. ISPs and large enterprises still use it heavily for this traffic engineering capability and for quality-of-service guarantees across their backbone, and also to run VPN services that keep many different customers' traffic logically isolated while sharing the same underlying physical infrastructure.
